extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning introductory proof techniques / discrete mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Worked solutions illustrating standard elementary proof techniques (pigeonhole, counting, parity, modular/divisibility arguments, direct/contrapositive/contradiction/case proofs) and combinatorial identities for use in solving and writing proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigeonhole principle
rubrics_metrics.description: If more objects are placed into fewer boxes than objects, some box contains at least two objects; used to force equal remainders or repeated outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: placing six integers into five boxes labeled by remainders mod 5 to show two share the same remainder; labeling six boxes for dice faces and using ceiling(n/6) to find the smallest n ensuring 10 occurrences of the same face; grouping rightmost digits into boxes (3,7), (2,8), (4,6), (1,9), (0), (5) to show among 7 numbers two have sum or difference multiple of 10.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication principle (rule of product)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count compound choices by multiplying counts for independent stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to count ways to choose committee members and leaders (choose k then choose 2 leaders gives C(n,k) * C(k,2)) and to count lists by choosing which positions differ and then filling them (used in deriving sum identities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting by fixing a distinguished element (middle or largest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count k-element subsets by conditioning on a distinguished element (e.g., the middle element or largest element) to obtain sum identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: count 3-element subsets of {0,...,n+1} by fixing middle element k; there are k(n+1−k) such sets, producing identity sum_{k=1}^n k(n+1−k) = C(n+2,3). Similarly, count subsets with largest element k to obtain sum_{k=m}^n C(k,m)=C(n+1,m+1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vandermonde / convolution identity via splitting a set
rubrics_metrics.description: Split a set S = A ∪ B with |A|=m, |B|=n and count p-element subsets by choosing k from A and p−k from B to derive ∑_{k=0}^p C(m,k) C(n,p−k) = C(m+n,p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret combinatorially: enumerate p-element subsets by how many elements they take from each part; sum over k.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial proofs of algebraic binomial identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove equalities of binomial/factorial expressions by interpreting both sides as counting the same combinatorial objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: C(2n,2)=2 C(n,2) + n^2 by splitting 2-element subsets by whether both elements lie in same half; C(n,k)C(k,2)=C(n,2)C(n−2,k−2) shown by two different selection orders (select full committee then leaders vs select leaders first).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complement pairing to show evenness of binomial coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Pair each n-element subset with its complement to produce pairs, showing counts are even.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for a 2n-element set, map each n-subset X to its complement X^c to pair subsets and conclude C(2n,n) is even.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting sequences / lists by number of special entries
rubrics_metrics.description: Count sequences of length n over an alphabet by conditioning on how many positions take certain symbols, yielding binomial-sum identities like ∑ 2^k C(n,k) = 3^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: count length-n lists from {a,b,c} by the number k of entries ≠ a: choose k positions (C(n,k)) and fill them with b or c (2^k), sum over k to get 3^n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division algorithm and gcd invariance under remainder
rubrics_metrics.description: If a = q b + r then gcd(a,b) = gcd(r,b); use division algorithm to reduce gcd computations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by expressing a and b in terms of gcd and showing gcd divides r and vice versa; basis for Euclidean algorithm reasoning used in solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity arguments using 2k and 2k+1 representations
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine even/odd nature of algebraic expressions, substitute x=2k or x=2k+1 and simplify to show expression has form 2m or 2m+1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used throughout: show x^2 even ⇒ x even (contrapositive), evaluate polynomials for parity, prove statements like 'a^3 + a^2 + a is even iff a is even' by substitution and case analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contrapositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove implication P ⇒ Q by proving ¬Q ⇒ ¬P, often cleaner when ¬Q has simpler structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for many number-theory/parity statements, e.g., 'if n^2 is even then n is even' and 'if 3 ∤ a then 3 ∤ a^2' style contrapositive reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the negation of the claim and derive an impossibility (often parity or divisibility contradiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in irrationality proofs: assume sqrt(2) or cube-root(3) rational, deduce both numerator and denominator divisible by prime, contradict reduced fraction assumption; also used to show impossibility statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Partition possibilities (often parity cases or whether quantities are zero/positive/negative) and prove the claim in each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common pattern for parity problems: consider a even/odd and b even/odd separately; used in multiple problems to exhaust possibilities and conclude the desired property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of modular arithmetic / prime divisibility in binomial coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: If p is prime and 0
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: p appears in p! but not in k! or (p−k)!, so p divides numerator of C(p,k). Useful in number-theoretic combinatorial proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic factorization to split equations into simpler factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Factor differences or sums (e.g., x^2−y^2 = (x−y)(x+y)) to reduce equations to product forms enabling case splits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: from x^2+5y = y^2+5x derive (x−y)(x+y)=5(x−y) and conclude x=y or x+y=5 by dividing by x−y when nonzero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairing arguments to demonstrate even counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Group combinatorial objects into unordered pairs to show the total count is even.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: list n-element subsets as X1,X1,X2,X2,... by pairing each subset with its complement, yielding an even total.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prime divisor lifting in irrationality proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that if a prime p divides a^k then p divides a; iterate to force both numerator and denominator divisible by p, contradicting reduced fraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to prove irrationality of roots: assume a/b in lowest terms, deduce prime divides both a and b, contradiction (examples for √2 and ∛3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting consecutive-integer products via coverage of small prime factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Show product of t consecutive integers is divisible by product of primes/factors up to t by noting the block must contain multiples of those factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: any 5 consecutive integers include multiples giving at least factors 5,4,3,2 (with two powers of 2), hence product divisible by 120; alternate viewpoint: C(n,5) is integer implies divisibility by 5!.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using factor parity and small-modulus analysis for Diophantine impossibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze possible remainders modulo small numbers (e.g., mod 4) of squares or sums to rule out integer solutions to certain equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint given for showing a^2 + b^2 = 3 c^2 has only trivial solution: inspect squares mod 4 and derive contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of elementary algebraic identities to lift congruences/powers
rubrics_metrics.description: From congruence a ≡ b (mod n) deduce a^k ≡ b^k (mod n) and related identities by algebraic factorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: if a ≡ b (mod n) then a^3 ≡ b^3 (mod n) via a^3−b^3 = (a−b)(a^2+ab+b^2); similarly a^2 ≡ ab (mod n) by multiplying a−b by a.
